fields.claim_quote: However, DNF-SAT is in L, by assigning variables to satisfy the first disjunct.
fields.explanation: The source instruction to satisfy the first disjunct fails on F=(x AND NOT x) OR x: its first term is impossible, but its second term is true at x=true. The Lean certificate establishes universal falsity of the first term and a satisfying assignment for F. This is a local error in the given justification. DNF-SAT membership in L remains true: scan the terms and accept when some term has no complementary literal pair; the needed term and literal positions can be stored with logarithmically many bits.
fields.flaw: The answer justifies DNF-SAT membership in L by assigning variables to satisfy the first disjunct. A satisfiable DNF can have a contradictory first disjunct, so this instruction need not be possible. This refutes the stated justification, not DNF-SAT membership in L.
fields.problem:
How to prove a problem is NOT NP-Complete?

Is there any general technique for proving a problem NOT being NP-Complete?

I got this question on the exam that asked me to show whether some problem (see below) is NP-Complete. I could not think of any real solution, and just proved it was in P. Obviously this is not a real answer.

NP-Complete is defined as the set of problems which are in NP, and all the NP problems can be reduced to it. So any proof should contradict at least one of these two conditions. This specific problem, is indeed in P (and thus in NP). So I am stuck with proving that there is some problem in NP that can't be reduced to this problem. How on the earth can this be proven??

Here is the specific problem I was given on exam:
>Let $DNF$ be the set of strings in [disjunctive normal form](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disjunctive_normal_form).
Let $DNFSAT$ be the language of strings from $DNF$ that are satisfiable by some assignment of variables. Show whether or not $DNFSAT$ is in NP-Complete.
fields.source_context:
0001 | Based on the comments, you seem to want an unconditional answer.
0002 | 
0003 | However, DNF-SAT is in L, by assigning variables to satisfy the first disjunct.  Hence if it is NP-complete, then L=NP.
0004 | 
0005 | On the other hand, if L = NP then DNF-SAT is NP-complete under logspace reductions, trivially.  (In fact, if L=NP then every problem in NP is NP-complete under logspace reductions.)
0006 | 
0007 | It follows that L=NP iff DNF-SAT is NP-complete under logspace reductions.
0008 | 
0009 | So you cannot currently make an unconditional statement that DNF-SAT is not NP-complete, as you seem to want to do.  It is not necessary to assume P≠NP, but the answer does have to be conditional on something, and L≠NP is the weakest possible hypothesis that guarantees the desired result.
fields.witness: Let F=(x AND NOT x) OR x. The first disjunct is false under both Boolean assignments, while F is true for x=true. Hence a satisfiable DNF need not admit an assignment satisfying its first disjunct. The selected Lean theorem proves exactly these facts. The source does not specify what an algorithm returns when the first disjunct is contradictory.
